features: WHO COULD GET IN, AND WHO COULD NOT — No migration: the database is not touched. Two opposite defects on the same theme: one kept the administrator out of their own system, the other opened a door to someone who should not get in.

UPGRADING FROM AN OLD VERSION NOW WORKS. Trying an upgrade from a beta.50, right after logging in came «500 — unknown column last_login_at», and there the road ended. It is a chicken and egg: that column comes from a migration, migrations are run from a page you reach after logging in, but the login itself wrote to that column. To upgrade the database you had to get in, and to get in you needed the database already upgraded — the only way out being a query by hand. Recording the last access is now treated for what it is, bookkeeping and not authentication: if it cannot be done, it does not stop you getting in.

CHECKED THAT THERE WERE NO OTHERS: we did not stop at the reported line but examined every table the upgrade changes or creates, and everything that runs before that page. There was only one, and from today an automated check redoes that path every run — it removes the column, performs a real login and demands that it work. No automated check had found this defect: it surfaced by trying the upgrade by hand on a copy.

THE CONFIGURATION FILE IS NO LONGER REWRITTEN BASED ON WHAT THE VISITOR ASKS FOR. Since v1.9 the program, on some hosts, added a line to its own configuration file saying «trust the proxy». It decided on every request, and decided by reading the site name as declared by whoever connects — something anyone can write as they please. On a configuration accepting any name, one unauthenticated visit was enough to make that line appear. And it also fired by mistake, because the comparison looked for a piece of text and not a domain: «studio.aversa.it», «condominio.avellino.it» and «mio.avvocato.it» triggered it with nobody trying.

WHY IT MATTERS: with that line active the program believes anyone who declares their own IP address, and the attempt limit rests on that address — five wrong passwords, or one wrong two-factor code, and access closes. By changing address on every attempt that limit never arrived, meaning a password or a six-digit code could be tried without end. Now a value is written that is safe everywhere: the program trusts only a proxy on the same internal network, never someone arriving from the internet. And since that value is fine everywhere, there is nothing left to guess: the part that looked at the site name was removed, not narrowed.

IF YOUR FILE HAD ALREADY BEEN CHANGED BY US IN THE PAST, the upgrade corrects it and writes it down for you: in place of the old line you find the explanation of what changed, why, and how to put the previous value back if your host really requires it. A line you wrote yourself is never touched, whatever its value. Finally, that check now runs only during installation and upgrade, no longer on every page anyone opens.

UNDER THE HOOD: seventeen new checks on trusted proxies, four of which do not test behaviour but that the defect cannot come back — that no reading of what the visitor sends reappears in that file, and that the dangerous value cannot be written again by inattention. Also, the script that prepares the downloadable package no longer rewrites the example configuration file: it regenerated it from scratch and they were two copies that could diverge, so much so that the generated copy promised something the program did not do.
